topics.title: Buy now, pay later: how a 'free' loan makes billions

demand.title: How 'Buy Now, Pay Later' Makes Billions From 'Free' Loans (WSJ)

topics.angle: If pay-in-four costs me nothing, who pays, and when does it start costing me?
topics.why_now: BNPL is one of the biggest long-form money subjects on YouTube: Grant Rudow's 'The Buy Now Pay Later Trap, Explained' has 6.04M views (and a 2.7M follow-up), How Money Works 1.55M, Modern MBA 1.13M, WSJ 1.93M. Holiday shopping (Black Friday) is five weeks out, when US viewers use it most. For 18-30-year-old US shoppers who split everything into four. A new category for the long feed (`bnpl`), outside the blocked credit_card window.
outline: hook: Rohan splits $300 sneakers into four $75 payments at checkout. 'Zero interest. Zero fees. So how is this a business worth billions?' The picture the video hangs on: a checkout button with a hidden pipe running from the shop's till to the lender
item 1, the shop pays: the merchant fee. $300 of BNPL shopping a month at a 5% fee is $15 a month, $180 a year, $900 over five years (fee_take), paid by the shop and built into prices
item 2, you buy more: Priya on why shops pay that fee (bigger baskets); Sikka grows with every click
recap-and-tease at ~2:30: the shop pays now. Next: the moment you start paying
item 3, the late fee: one missed $75 instalment and the fee schedule (verify the provider caps)
item 4, the longer plans: the same 'pay over time' button on a $1,500 laptop at 30% APR for 12 months is $146 a month, $255 in interest (emi)
item 5, stacking: four plans with four apps, four due dates; the calendar fills up
recap-and-tease at ~6:00: the biggest cost isn't a fee at all
item 6 (strongest, ~2/3 in): what the $300 a month would have become: invested at an assumed 8% for 10 years it is $55,250 (sip)
ending: Sharma Uncle's rule for the button; how the business really works in one picture; disclaimer end card
topics.maths: fee_take ($300 a month, 5% merchant fee, 12 a year, 5 years), emi ($1,500 at 30% for 12 months), sip ($300 a month, 8% assumed, 10 years); compare for the two biggest numbers
verify: Merchant fees for BNPL of 'as much as 5%' (WSJ, the providers' own merchant pricing pages)
Late fee amounts and caps of a named provider, or say 'late fees' without a figure
Longer BNPL plans can charge interest up to around 30-36% APR (provider disclosures, CFPB)
8% is an assumed long-run return, said as one

topics.title: Once you understand where your salary goes, you'll stop waiting for a raise

demand.title: FAMILY SALARY CYCLE || Middle Class Family (Sumit Bhyan)

topics.angle: Why does a ₹60,000 salary disappear by the 20th, and what does the month look like once you see it?
topics.why_now: The salary-cycle skit is the biggest middle-class money video in India (38.9M, a 14-minute sketch), and it fits our cast-led skits exactly. Warikoo's 'Escaping the Middle Class Trap' (2.87M) and Nishant Patel (2.42M) show the 'why am I still broke' search is huge. Takes the subject (a month of salary), not the treatment: our version follows one month in chapters with computed numbers. For 22-32-year-olds on their first or second salary. Category `budgeting` is not blocked.
outline: hook: day 1, the salary SMS lands; day 20, Rohan checks his balance and hides the phone from Priya. 'Here is where every rupee went.' The picture the video hangs on: a calendar wall, one page torn off per chapter, money draining out of a tank
day 1-3, the fixed bills: rent, the bike EMI: ₹1,00,000 at 12% for 3 years is ₹3,321 a month, ₹19,572 in interest (emi)
day 5, the phone EMI: ₹1.2 lakh phone at 16% over a year is ₹10,888 a month, ₹10,652 just for the wait (emi)
recap-and-tease at ~2:30: two EMIs took a quarter of the month. Next: the cost nobody budgets
day 10, the quiet raise in prices: ₹40,000 of monthly living costs at 6% inflation is ₹71,634 in 10 years (price_rise), so a raise that matches prices leaves you exactly here
day 15, the 'safe' savings: ₹1 lakh in a 7% FD with 6% inflation earns a real 0.9% a year (real_return)
recap-and-tease at ~6:00: Sharma Uncle has seen this month thirty years in a row; what he did differently is one line
day 20 (strongest, ~2/3 in): the ₹6,000 that was left on day 1: ₹6,000 a month for 20 years at an assumed 12% is ₹59.9 lakh (sip), ₹45.5 lakh of it gains
day 30: the same month replayed with the ₹6,000 moved to day 1; Priya, Sikka cheers
ending: 'Once you understand the cycle, the raise is not the answer, the order is.' Comment your day-20 balance; disclaimer end card
topics.maths: emi x2 (bike ₹1 L 12% 3y; phone ₹1.2 L 16% 1y), price_rise (₹40,000/month, 6%, 10y), real_return (₹1 L, 7% FD, 6% inflation, 10y), sip (₹6,000/month, 12% assumed, 20y)
verify: Two-wheeler loan rates around 10-14% and consumer-durable/phone EMI rates around 14-18% at Indian lenders (lender rate pages)
FD rates of 6-7.5% at large banks; 6% inflation is an assumption, said as one
12% is an assumed long-run equity return, never a promise

topics.title: Rich vs poor: why $100,000 of salary pays 2.5× the tax of $100,000 of gains

demand.title: How the rich avoid paying taxes (Vox)

topics.angle: Why does the same $100,000 get taxed so differently depending on whether you work for it or own something that earns it?
topics.why_now: 'How the rich avoid taxes' is a proven long subject: Vox 3.9M, Grant Cardone 2.9M, How Money Works 1.7M. US tax season content peaks Jan-Apr but this is evergreen. Education only (how the US code treats wages vs long-term gains), never 'how to avoid tax'. For US salaried 22-35-year-olds. Category `tax` is not blocked.
outline: hook: Rohan and Sharma Uncle both 'earn' $100,000 this year. Rohan's tax: $13,170. Sharma's: $5,168. The picture the video hangs on: two identical stacks of cash walking through two different doors, one a turnstile that takes a slice, one a revolving door
item 1, wages: the brackets explained band by band; $100,000 of salary pays $13,170, 13.2% effective, 22% on the last dollar (income_tax_bands, 2026 single, standard deduction)
item 2, the payroll slice: 7.65% FICA on wages is another $7,650 that gains never pay (fee_take)
recap-and-tease at ~2:30: the salary door takes two slices. Next: the other door
item 3, long-term gains: the 0% band up to $49,450 of taxable income, then 15%: $100,000 of gains pays $5,168, 5.2% (income_tax_bands)
item 4, the gap: $8,002 a year, 2.5× (compare)
recap-and-tease at ~6:00: the rich also have a way to spend without selling

item 5 (strongest, ~2/3 in): buy, borrow, die explained: borrowing $100,000 against assets at 6% costs $3,280 in interest for a year (emi) and no income tax; Priya explains why that works only with assets
item 6: what the rest of us can actually use: tax-advantaged accounts named only to explain them (401(k), IRA), no recommendation
ending: the two doors side by side; which door does your money go through? Disclaimer end card
topics.maths: income_tax_bands x2 (wages: allowance 16,100, 2026 single brackets shifted by the deduction; gains: allowance 16,100, 0% to 65,550 gross, 15% to 561,600, 20% above), fee_take (7.65% FICA on $100,000, 1 period), compare (wage tax vs gains tax), emi ($100,000 at 6% for 12 months)
verify: 2026 single standard deduction $16,100 and single brackets 10/12/22/24/32/35/37% with tops 12,400 / 50,400 / 105,700 / 201,775 / 256,225 / 640,600 of taxable income (IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-32; my bands assume these, the writer must confirm)
2026 long-term capital gains 0% up to $49,450 and 15% up to $545,500 taxable income, single (IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-32; Kiplinger)
FICA: 6.2% Social Security + 1.45% Medicare on wages (ssa.gov / irs.gov)
The script must say it ignores state tax, NIIT and the wage cap, and that gains stacked on top of a salary are taxed differently
